Agent.text:
I built Cutline, a dark-themed desktop video editor where FFmpeg does every edit, and it passes Craft Anything's checks.

You drop in videos and they line up back to back in alphabetical order, with "clip 2" before "clip 10". You can rearrange them by dragging in the list or on the timeline, or put them back with the A-Z button. On the right you pick the format (MP4 by default, plus 10 others or any type you enter), the final picture size, and how many equal-length parts to make. Each part has its own maximum size, 20 MB by default, and the "View console" switch shows every FFmpeg command and its output as it runs.

I tested it here on Linux with real videos. A robot dragged files onto the window, reordered them, typed a 5 MB limit for one part and exported. All parts came out under their limits (19.4, 4.8 and 18.5 MB) and nearly equal in length, about 0.1 seconds longer than an exact third. The other formats and GIFs also stayed under their limits.

Things to know:
- **Windows and Mac:** the app builds for both but hasn't been run on a real Windows PC or Mac yet. That's the main thing still unknown.
- **Preview:** it plays without sound.
- **"Size for the final video":** I read this as the picture size (like 1080p). The file-size limit covers the other meaning.

A good next thing to ask for would be trimming the start and end of each clip, or sound in the preview.

Agent.text:
Yes, you can now cut out stretches. Move the playhead to where the unwanted bit starts and press "Mark start", move to where it ends and press "Mark end", then press "Remove". Each cut leaves a red marker on the timeline that you can click to put the stretch back, and Undo or Ctrl+Z also reverses the last cut.

I tested it in the real window: removing an 8.4-second stretch from 28 seconds of video gave a 19.6-second export, and splitting into parts and the size limits use only what's left. It still hasn't been tried on a real Windows PC or Mac.
